abstracts.abstract: Traditional cost-based query optimization relies on models designed for centralized databases, which fundamentally fail to capture the complexities of modern heterogeneous distributed database systems. This paper introduces a novel information-theoretic framework that provides the first unified theoretical foundation for understanding query optimization across distributed environments with varying network topologies, data distributions, and processing capabilities. We formalize query optimization as a conditional entropy minimization problem, where the uncertainty in data placement, network conditions, and processing loads are treated as first-class citizens in the cost model. Our framework enables rigorous analysis of the complexity landscape, revealing that optimal query planning in heterogeneous distributed systems requires fundamentally different algorithmic approaches than those employed in traditional query optimizers. We prove that optimal plans must explicitly balance information-theoretic communication costs against local processing efficiency, and we derive polynomial-time algorithms achieving constant-factor approximations to theoretically optimal plans. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world workloads validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating 40-70% reduction in query execution time compared to state-of-the-art distributed query optimizers across diverse network conditions and data distributions. This work opens new research directions in adaptive query optimization and provides a principled foundation for designing next-generation distributed database systems.

Concurrency control protocols constitute critical infrastructure in modern database systems, yet traditional analysis techniques fail to accurately characterize performance under contention. This paper presents a rigorous queueing-theoretic analysis of multi-version concurrency control that yields improved theoretical understanding and substantially tighter performance bounds. We develop a formal model that captures the relationship between version management overhead, conflict rates, and transaction abort probability, enabling precise characterization of optimal version configuration strategies. Our analysis reveals that existing heuristics for version retention and garbage collection are fundamentally suboptimal, leading to degraded performance under high-contention workloads. We prove that optimal version management follows a threshold-based policy, achieving near-optimal performance while requiring only logarithmic space overhead. We measure performance improvements through rigorous complexity analysis and conduct extensive experiments, demonstrating that our theoretically-grounded algorithms achieve up to 65% improvement in transaction throughput compared to production database systems. The analytical framework extends naturally to related problems including read/write optimization and workload-aware configuration tuning. This work provides both the theoretical tools for understanding MVCC behavior and practical algorithms that significantly advance the state of the art in transaction processing.

The memory wall presents a fundamental challenge to continued performance scaling in in-memory database systems. We present Pillar, a novel in-memory database architecture that fundamentally reimagines the relationship between processing and storage through near-data processing. Unlike conventional designs that treat compute and memory as separate tiers connected by a bus, Pillar co-designs hardware and software to execute query processing operations directly within or adjacent to memory modules, effectively eliminating data movement as a performance bottleneck. Pillar introduces three key architectural innovations: a memory-augmented processing substrate that supports computation within memory arrays, a dataflow-oriented execution model that minimizes control overhead while maximizing parallelism, and a novel transaction mechanism specifically designed for near-data processing that maintains ACID properties without traditional write-ahead logging. This paradigm shift enables sub-microsecond query latencies and millions of operations per second, representing 10-100x improvement over state-of-the-art in-memory databases. We implement Pillar using a combination of FPGA prototypes and software simulation, validating the architecture across OLTP, OLAP, and HTAP workloads. The complete system demonstrates that near-data processing represents a viable and transformative approach to designing future data management systems, providing a concrete blueprint for achieving orders-of-magnitude performance improvements in real-time data processing applications.

Graph databases face inherent performance challenges when processing complex queries on large-scale property graphs due to irregular data access patterns that stress conventional storage layouts. We present GraphX, a distributed graph database system that introduces a novel storage organization and query execution engine specifically optimized for property graph workloads. GraphX employs a hierarchical partitioning strategy that preserves graph locality while achieving balanced distribution across cluster nodes, combined with a carefully designed caching mechanism that captures intermediate traversal results based on graph connectivity patterns. The query execution engine introduces a pipelined operator model that avoids materialization overhead in multi-hop traversals, substantially reducing latency for complex graph pattern matching queries. We describe detailed implementation strategies including dynamic workload-aware partitioning adjustments and adaptive caching policies that respond to evolving query patterns. Extensive evaluation on graphs containing billions of edges demonstrates that GraphX achieves 5-20x speedup on traversal queries and 2-8x speedup on graph analytics workloads compared to Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, and JanusGraph, while maintaining compatibility with standard graph query languages. GraphX provides a practical path to scaling property graph databases for demanding enterprise applications.
